groups.high: In Bangladesh, section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 supplies default termination rules only where no contrary contract, local law, or usage applies. Agricultural or manufacturing leases are treated as yearly tenancies terminable by six months' notice expiring at the end of a tenancy year. Leases for other purposes are treated as monthly tenancies terminable by fifteen days' notice expiring at the end of a tenancy month. Commercial use alone does not place every lease in the six-month category. Notice must be written, signed by or for the giver, and served through the permitted methods. Ending a contractual tenancy does not automatically authorize physical eviction: Bangladesh's applicable rent-control protections, legal grounds, and court procedures must also be considered. International housing standards emphasize adequate notice, consultation, access to remedies, and protection against arbitrary forced eviction, rather than one universal notice period. Keep the lease, notice, payment records, and service evidence. Seek prompt local legal advice if removal, a lockout, threats, or utility disconnection is proposed; do not assume that a notice alone settles the right to possession.
groups.mid: In Bangladesh, section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882 gives default notice rules. They apply only if no different contract, local law, or custom applies. A lease for farming or manufacturing is treated as yearly. It can end with six months' notice that expires at the end of a tenancy year. A lease for another purpose is treated as monthly. It can end with fifteen days' notice that expires at the end of a tenancy month. A shop or other business does not always count as manufacturing. The notice must be written, signed by or for the person giving it, and served in a permitted way. A notice ending a lease does not itself let an owner throw someone out. Rent-control protection, lawful grounds, and court steps may still apply. International housing standards call for proper notice, consultation, ways to challenge the action, and protection from arbitrary forced eviction. They do not set one worldwide notice period. Keep your lease, notice, rent records, and proof of service. Get local legal advice quickly about a lockout, threats, removal, or cut utilities. A notice alone does not decide who may take possession.
groups.low: Bangladesh has default rules for ending a lease in section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act 1882. A different contract, local law, or custom may change them. For farming or manufacturing, the default lease is yearly. It needs six months' notice ending with the tenancy year. For other uses, the default is monthly. It needs fifteen days' notice ending with a tenancy month. Not every shop or business is manufacturing. The notice must be in writing and signed by or for the giver. It must be served in a way the law allows. But a notice does not let an owner throw you out. Rent-control rights, legal grounds, and court steps may still apply. World housing standards call for proper notice and consultation. People need ways to challenge an eviction and protection from forced, arbitrary removal. There is no single world notice period. Keep the lease, notice, rent records, and proof of how notice was served. Get local legal help soon if there are threats, a lockout, a plan to remove you, or cut utilities. A notice alone does not settle the right to take the home back.
groups.source_review: Checked Bangladesh section 106 directly, rent-control possession protection, and OHCHR eviction standards.
groups.notes: Corrected manufacturing/commercial classification, omitted contractual defaults and tenancy-end timing, and notice/eviction conflation.

groups.high: Security-deposit rules are jurisdiction-specific; there is no verified universal UN-Habitat rule requiring return within fourteen to thirty days. A lawful deposit generally secures defined tenancy obligations rather than becoming the landlord's money automatically. Permitted deductions, refund deadlines, deposit protection, interest, and dispute procedures depend on governing law and the agreement. Ordinary wear from reasonable use should be distinguished from tenant-caused damage; repair claims should consider evidence, causation, age, and condition rather than fund an unjustified new replacement. Unpaid rent can also be a permitted deduction in some systems. For example, GOV.UK guidance for relevant protected deposits requires return within ten days after both sides agree the amount, not simply ten days after moving out. Bangladesh's Premises Rent Control Act 1991 separately restricts deposits and advance rent, with specific exceptions, so foreign deposit practice must not be presented as Bangladeshi law. Keep inventories, dated photographs, receipts, the agreement, and correspondence. Request an itemized account and repayment in writing. Use the applicable deposit scheme, housing authority, or court process if disputed; compensation or penalties are not automatic everywhere.
groups.mid: Deposit rules depend on where you rent. There is no proven world UN-Habitat rule for return within fourteen to thirty days. A lawful deposit covers set duties under the lease. It is not free money for the owner. Local law and the lease set the deadline and allowed costs. They also set rules for deposit schemes, interest, and disputes. Normal wear from fair use differs from damage you caused. Ask for proof of damage and costs. The item's age and condition matter. You should not always pay the full new price for an old item. Some laws also allow sums for unpaid rent. GOV.UK gives an example for relevant protected deposits. The money is due within ten days after both sides agree the amount. This is not just ten days after you leave. Bangladesh's 1991 rent law has its own limits on deposits and advance rent, with exceptions. A foreign rule may not apply. Keep the lease, item lists, dated photos, receipts, and messages. Ask in writing for a list of deductions and repayment. Use the right deposit scheme, housing office, or court for disputes. Extra damages or fines are not automatic.
groups.low: Deposit rules depend on where you rent. There is no one world UN-Habitat rule for return in fourteen to thirty days. A lawful deposit covers set duties in the lease. It is not free money for the owner. The law and lease set the date for return. They set what can be kept, interest, and dispute rules too. Normal wear is not damage you caused. Ask for proof of the harm and cost. An item's age and state matter. You should not always pay a full new price for an old item. Some places allow sums for unpaid rent. GOV.UK gives one example for relevant protected deposits. Return is due ten days after both sides agree the sum, not just after you leave. Bangladesh's 1991 rent law has other limits on deposits and advance rent, with exceptions. A foreign rule may not apply. Keep the lease, item list, dated photos, receipts, and messages. Ask in writing for a list of charges and repayment. A deposit scheme, housing office, or court may help with a dispute. Extra payments or fines are not automatic.
groups.source_review: Checked UK example and Bangladesh deposit/advance restrictions. No substantiated named UN-Habitat universal refund instrument found.
groups.notes: Removed invented worldwide deadline, interest, damages entitlement, and deposit-only-for-damage claim.

groups.high: Section 21 of Bangladesh's Premises Rent Control Act 1991 distinguishes ordinary repairs, urgent work, and a special habitability provision. For covered ordinary obligations, a tenant may apply to the Controller, who can direct the landlord to repair. If the landlord fails within thirty days after the statutory notice, the tenant can seek permission with an estimated cost. Written permission specifies the authorized amount. Recovery is generally limited to that amount and one-sixth of the year's rent; excess expenditure is borne by the tenant. For urgent repairs where procedural delay risks personal harm or serious inconvenience, the tenant serves the prescribed notice requesting completion within seventy-two hours and simultaneously submits a copy and estimate to the Controller. If the landlord fails, the tenant may undertake the work, submit accounts, and recover the amount determined by the Controller, subject to the urgent-route one-sixth annual cap. Subsection 21(5) contains a distinct rule for repairs without which occupation or use becomes extremely difficult; its application needs case-specific advice. Do not assume merely calling a repair urgent authorizes unlimited rent withholding. Preserve notice, estimates, photographs, and invoices, and obtain qualified advice before deductions.
groups.mid: Section 21 of Bangladesh's 1991 rent law has routes for ordinary and urgent repairs. It also has a special rule for a home that is very hard to live in or use. For ordinary covered work, ask the Controller to order the owner to repair. If the owner fails within thirty days after the notice, ask permission to do it. Send a cost estimate. Written permission sets the allowed sum. You can generally recover no more than that sum or one-sixth of the year's rent. You bear extra costs. Urgent work must involve risk of personal harm or serious inconvenience from delay. Serve the proper notice asking the owner to act within seventy-two hours. Send its copy and cost estimate to the Controller at the same time. If the owner fails, you may do the work. Then send accounts. The Controller decides what costs you can recover. This urgent route has a one-sixth annual rent cap. Section 21(5) has a distinct rule for extreme difficulty living in or using the home. Ask for advice on it. Calling work urgent does not permit unlimited rent withholding. Keep notices, estimates, photos, and bills. Get local advice before deductions.
groups.low: Section 21 of Bangladesh's 1991 rent law deals with repairs. It has steps for ordinary and urgent work. A special rule covers a home that is very hard to live in or use. For ordinary covered work, ask the Controller to order the owner to act. If work is not done within thirty days after the notice, ask leave to do it. Send a cost estimate. Written permission sets the sum allowed. You can generally recover no more than that sum or one-sixth of the year's rent. Extra costs are yours. Urgent work must risk personal harm or serious inconvenience from delay. Serve the right notice. Ask for work within seventy-two hours. Send a copy and estimate to the Controller at once. If the owner fails, you may do the work. Send the bills. The Controller sets the sum you can recover. This route has a one-sixth yearly rent cap. Section 21(5) is a distinct rule for extreme trouble living in or using the home. Ask for advice on it. Urgent does not mean you may withhold rent without limit. Keep notices, estimates, photos, and bills. Get local help before deductions.
groups.source_review: Read all eight subsections directly in official Bangla. Special subsection (5) flagged for case-specific application rather than oversimplified as unlimited urgent recovery.
groups.notes: Added missing thirty-day/permission and seventy-two-hour/Controller-copy procedures; corrected universal discretionary cap override.

groups.high: A landlord's deliberate disconnection of water, electricity, or other essential services to force a tenant out can constitute coercive self-help eviction. OHCHR describes utility interference used to make continued occupation impossible as a forced-eviction concern. The appropriate legal remedy and any criminal penalty depend on domestic law, not a single worldwide offence. In Bangladesh, section 24 of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991 addresses specified intentional interference with amenities or contracted supplies where section 18 protects against possession orders, subject to its stated exceptions. A genuine safety shutdown, utility-provider action, repair necessity, and coercive landlord action must be distinguished. Record dates, messages, bills, outage details, and any health effects; ask the provider whether the interruption concerns the wider supply. Seek urgent legal or housing-authority help for restoration or protective orders where available, and contact emergency services if there is immediate danger. Do not reconnect gas or electricity yourself. A cutoff does not automatically cancel every later possession case, nor does it guarantee compensation. Continue observing lawful payment and procedural obligations while obtaining advice.
groups.mid: An owner should not cut water, power, or other key services to force a tenant out. OHCHR treats this as a forced-eviction concern. Local law decides the remedy and any crime or fine. There is no single world penalty. Section 24 of Bangladesh's 1991 rent law covers some deliberate cuts to services or amenities. It applies where section 18 protects the tenancy. Its conditions and exceptions matter. A real safety shutdown is different from pressure to leave. So are needed repairs or a utility firm's action. Keep dates, messages, bills, and details of the outage. Note any harm to health. Ask the provider if the wider supply is affected. Seek urgent local legal or housing-office help. An order to restore service may be possible. Call emergency services for immediate danger. Do not reconnect gas or power yourself. A cut does not automatically cancel a later possession case. Nor does it guarantee damages. Keep meeting lawful rent and legal steps while getting advice.
groups.low: An owner should not cut water, power, or other key services to force you out. OHCHR treats this as a forced-eviction concern. Local law sets the help, crime, or fine. There is no one world penalty. Section 24 of Bangladesh's 1991 rent law covers some deliberate cuts to services or amenities. Section 18 must protect the tenancy. Conditions and exceptions apply. A real safety shutdown is different from a threat to leave. So is a needed repair. The utility firm may cause an outage too. Keep dates, messages, bills, and details of the cut. Note any harm to health. Ask if the wider area has lost supply. Get urgent local legal or housing-office help. An order may restore service. Call emergency services for immediate danger. Do not reconnect gas or power yourself. A cut does not cancel every later possession case. Payment for harm is not certain. Keep following lawful rent and legal steps while getting advice.
groups.source_review: Checked OHCHR forced-eviction account and Bangladesh section 24 with conditions. No universal damages or automatic invalidation inferred.
groups.notes: Qualified domestic remedies, exceptions and penalty scope; removed claim that all subsequent proceedings automatically fail.

groups.high: A claim that rent everywhere may rise only 10% every two years with three months' notice needs a specific jurisdiction and provision. Bangladesh's Premises Rent Control Act 1991 does not establish that simple universal formula. Section 7 restricts increases above standard rent, subject to the Act. Section 15 provides for the Controller to determine standard annual rent using 15% of the property's market value as assessed under prescribed rules. Section 16 allows redetermination on application every two years; this is not a 10% biennial cap. Sections 8 and 9 address specified improvements or supplied furniture and certain taxes or charges. Lease terms, applicability, and the statutory process must be checked before demanding or accepting a change. Ask for the proposed amount, basis, effective date, and notice in writing. Keep the lease, payment records, and any standard-rent order. A tenant should obtain local advice about challenging an excessive demand or applying to the Controller, rather than stop payment or assume an unsupported three-month notice rule settles the dispute.
groups.mid: Do not assume rent can rise only 10% every two years with three months' notice. That claim needs a named law and place. Bangladesh's Premises Rent Control Act 1991 does not set that simple rule. Section 7 limits increases above standard rent, subject to the Act. Under section 15, the Controller sets standard yearly rent using 15% of the property's market value assessed by the prescribed rules. Section 16 allows a fresh decision on application every two years. That is not a 10% rise limit. Sections 8 and 9 deal with certain improvements, furniture, taxes, or charges. Check the lease, whether the law applies, and the required steps before changing rent. Ask for the new amount, reason, start date, and notice in writing. Keep your lease, receipts, and any standard-rent order. Get local advice about challenging too much rent or asking the Controller to decide it. Do not stop paying or rely on an unverified three-month notice rule alone.
groups.low: A 10% rent rise every two years is not a rule for all places. Nor is three months' notice. Check the law for your home. Bangladesh's 1991 rent law has different rules. Section 7 limits rises above standard rent, subject to the Act. Under section 15, the Controller sets standard yearly rent. It is 15% of the home's market value found under the set rules. Section 16 allows a new decision on application every two years. It is not a 10% rise cap. Sections 8 and 9 cover some improvements, furniture, taxes, and charges. Check the lease. Check if the law applies. Follow the right steps. Ask in writing for the new sum, reason, and start date. Keep the lease, receipts, and any standard-rent order. Ask a local adviser how to challenge excess rent or apply to the Controller. Do not just stop paying. Do not rely on an unverified three-month notice rule.
groups.source_review: Checked sections 7–9, 15–16 in Bangladesh official Act. Unsupported original cap/notice replaced rather than fabricated.
groups.notes: Corrected invented 10% biennial/three-month notice mandate and preserved true two-year redetermination distinction.

groups.high: Tenant privacy and access rules depend on governing law and the lease. A landlord's ownership does not mean unrestricted entry, and legitimate inspection or repairs must be balanced against the tenant's occupation and privacy. A twenty-four-hour notice rule applies in some jurisdictions and contracts, including the example summarized by GOV.UK, but is not a universal term of every lease. Bangladesh's Transfer of Property Act section 108(m), subject to contrary contract or usage, refers to access at reasonable times for inspection; it does not itself establish a general twenty-four-hour rule. The Rent Controller's inspection power under section 6 of the Premises Rent Control Act has its own forty-eight-hour written-notice safeguard for entry without occupant permission. That official inspection rule is distinct from a private landlord's ordinary access. Genuine emergencies such as fire, serious flooding, or a suspected gas hazard may justify immediate protective access under applicable rules, not unlimited later visits. Arrange purpose, time, notice, and consent in writing where possible. Record repeated unannounced entries and seek local advice about harassment or unsafe conduct.
groups.mid: An owner does not have unlimited access to your home. The law and lease balance repairs and checks with your privacy. Some places or contracts need twenty-four hours' notice. GOV.UK gives one such example. It is not a rule for all leases. Section 108(m) of Bangladesh's Transfer of Property Act deals with access at reasonable times for inspections. A different contract or custom can apply. The section does not set a general twenty-four-hour rule. A Rent Controller's inspection is different. Section 6 of Bangladesh's 1991 rent law has a forty-eight-hour written-notice safeguard. This applies to entry without the occupier's permission. Do not treat it as the owner's ordinary access rule. A real fire, serious flood, or gas hazard may justify urgent protective entry under local rules. That does not allow unlimited visits later. Where possible, agree purpose, time, notice, and consent in writing. Record repeated surprise visits. Get local advice about harassment or unsafe acts.
groups.low: An owner cannot assume they may enter your home at any time. Your privacy matters. Law and lease rules cover repairs and checks. Some places or contracts need twenty-four hours' notice. GOV.UK gives an example. This is not a rule for every home. In Bangladesh, section 108(m) of the Transfer of Property Act refers to inspections at reasonable times. A different contract or custom may apply. It does not set a general twenty-four-hour rule. A Rent Controller has a separate power to inspect. Section 6 of the 1991 rent law has a forty-eight-hour written-notice safeguard. It applies to entry without the occupier's permission. It is not the owner's normal visit rule. A real fire, serious flood, or gas danger may need urgent protective entry under local rules. This does not allow any visit later. Where possible, agree in writing why and when a visit will happen. Include notice and consent. Note repeated surprise entries. Get local advice on harassment, threats, or unsafe conduct.
groups.source_review: Checked UK example, Bangladesh section 108(m), and distinct Controller inspection provision.
groups.notes: Corrected universal notice rule and separated private access from official inspection.

groups.high: Section 13 of Bangladesh's Premises Rent Control Act 1991 requires a landlord, upon rent payment, immediately to provide the tenant with a signed receipt in the prescribed form and to retain its counterfoil. This is a legal record of receipt, not merely a courtesy. A useful payment record identifies the payer, property, amount, payment date, and rental period, consistent with the prescribed requirements. Keep receipts with the agreement and other payment evidence, such as bank or mobile-transfer records. A transfer record may support proof but should not be assumed automatically to replace the required signed receipt. If a receipt is refused, request it in writing and preserve evidence of payment and refusal. Seek local advice on the applicable complaint or rent-deposit process if payment itself is rejected; do not stop paying without understanding the consequences. Missing a receipt does not mean a tenant can never prove payment or that a court automatically shifts every burden of proof. The Act separately provides for consequences of receipt-related noncompliance, with procedural conditions. Do not invent loan eligibility effects or a blanket prohibition on all electronic evidence.
groups.mid: Section 13 of Bangladesh's 1991 rent law says the owner must give a signed receipt as soon as rent is paid. It must use the prescribed form. The owner must keep its counterfoil too. This is a legal record, not just a favour. A clear receipt shows who paid, the home, sum, date, and rent period, in line with the set form. Keep it with your lease and other proof. Bank or mobile-transfer records may help. But do not assume they replace the signed receipt required by law. If the owner refuses a receipt, ask in writing. Keep proof that you paid and asked. If the owner refuses payment too, get local advice on the proper complaint or rent-deposit route. Do not stop paying without checking risks. Losing a receipt does not mean you cannot prove payment another way. It does not make every court burden shift automatically. The law has separate rules on failure to give receipts. Proper steps apply. Do not assume all electronic proof is barred.
groups.low: In Bangladesh, ask for a signed receipt each time you pay rent. Section 13 of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991 says the owner must give it at once in the set form. The owner must keep the counterfoil too. A receipt is proof of payment, not just a favour. It should show who paid, the home, sum, date, and rent period, as the set form requires. Keep it with the lease. Keep bank or mobile-transfer proof too. That proof may help, but it may not replace the signed receipt required by law. If the owner will not give one, ask in writing. Keep proof that you paid and asked. If the owner will not take rent, ask a local adviser about the right complaint or rent-deposit steps. Do not just stop paying. A lost receipt does not mean there is no other proof. It does not shift every court rule against one side. The Act has rules for receipt failures, with steps to follow. Do not assume all electronic proof is banned.
groups.source_review: Read official section 13 including immediate issue and counterfoil. Additional recordkeeping is practical advice, not invented statutory form fields.
groups.notes: Removed absolute paper-only and automatic burden-shifting claims; added counterfoil.

groups.high: In Bangladesh, section 18(1)(b) of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991 identifies unauthorized subletting of the premises or any part, in the absence of a contrary contract, as an exception to ordinary protection against possession orders. The relevant provision is not section 13, which concerns receipts. Do not assume that renting out a room is automatically exempt because only whole-premises subletting matters. Obtain the landlord's written consent or confirm an express contractual permission before creating a subtenancy. Keep the scope, area, use, duration, and conditions clear, and check other lease and legal requirements. Unauthorized subletting can expose the original tenant to legal proceedings, but does not authorize immediate lockout or establish that every sublease is automatically void with no possible rights. Section 18(3) provides specified protection for some lawful subtenants when the original tenancy ends, subject to its conditions and exceptions. The original tenant may remain responsible for obligations under the lease. Distinguish a guest, shared occupation, assignment, and a genuine subtenancy using the actual facts. Obtain local advice before relying on an oral arrangement or removing an occupant.
groups.mid: In Bangladesh, section 18(1)(b) of the 1991 rent law covers subletting without the owner's written consent. A contrary contract can matter. The rule covers all or any part of the home. It is not section 13, which concerns receipts. One room is not automatically exempt. Get written consent or check for express contract permission before a subtenancy. Record the area, use, duration, and terms. Check other lease and legal rules. Unauthorized subletting may lead to possession proceedings. It does not allow an instant lockout. Nor does it prove every sublease is void or every subtenant lacks rights. Section 18(3) protects some lawful subtenants when the main lease ends. Conditions and exceptions apply. The original tenant may still owe duties under the lease. A guest, shared home, lease transfer, and subtenancy can differ. Check the facts with a local adviser before relying on spoken consent or removing an occupant.
groups.low: Check before you rent your home or a room to someone else. In Bangladesh, section 18(1)(b) of the 1991 rent law covers all or part let without the owner's written consent. A different contract may apply. Section 13 is about receipts, not subletting. One room is not always exempt. Get written consent or check for clear permission in the lease. Do this first. Record the part let, use, length, and terms. Check other lease and legal rules too. Subletting without consent may lead to a court claim for possession. It does not allow an instant lockout. It does not mean every sublease is void or that no subtenant has rights. Section 18(3) protects some lawful subtenants when the main lease ends. Its conditions and exceptions matter. The first tenant may still owe lease duties. A guest, sharing, lease transfer, and subtenancy can differ. Ask a local adviser to check the facts. Do so before relying on spoken consent or trying to remove someone.
groups.source_review: Read Bangladesh section 18(1)(b) and 18(3), with general transfer obligations under section 108.
groups.notes: Corrected section number, partial-subletting exemption, and automatic total loss of subtenant rights.

groups.high: In Bangladesh, standard rent under section 15 of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991 is determined by the Controller on application by either landlord or tenant. The statutory annual amount is 15% of the property's market value assessed under the prescribed method, subject to the Act's treatment of existing determinations. It is not simply the average advertised rent of nearby flats or a discretionary five-year rent-history formula. Under section 16, when the application results in a change, the standard rent is payable from the month immediately after the application date. Redetermination can be sought every two years. Section 7 restricts increases above standard rent, subject to the Act, and other provisions address permitted additions or adjustments. Keep the lease, receipts, any earlier order, and evidence relevant to the property's assessment. Both sides should have the statutory opportunity to respond. Ask the Controller's office or a qualified adviser about jurisdiction, required documents, filing costs, and review or appeal deadlines. Do not unilaterally reduce rent based only on neighboring listings or assume an order always starts on its issue date.
groups.mid: In Bangladesh, either a tenant or landlord can ask the Controller to set standard rent under section 15 of the Premises Rent Control Act 1991. The Act uses 15% of the property's market value as the yearly amount, with that value assessed under the prescribed method. It also deals with earlier rent decisions. This is not just the average rent in nearby adverts or a five-year rent-history rule. Section 16 says that if the application changes the rent, the new standard rent starts in the month just after the application date. A fresh decision can be sought every two years. Section 7 limits rises above standard rent, subject to the Act. Other rules deal with allowed additions or adjustments. Keep your lease, receipts, old orders, and evidence for the property's assessment. Both sides should have the proper chance to respond. Ask the Controller's office or a local legal adviser which office to use, what papers and costs are required, and when to seek review or appeal. Do not cut rent yourself based only on adverts. An order does not always start on the day it is issued.
groups.low: In Bangladesh, an owner or tenant can ask the Controller to set standard rent. Section 15 of the 1991 rent law gives the rule. The yearly sum is 15% of the home's market value found by the set method. Earlier orders may matter. It is not just nearby rents in adverts. There is no simple five-year rent-history rule. Under section 16, a changed rent starts in the month just after the application date. A new decision can be sought every two years. Section 7 limits rises above standard rent, subject to the Act. Other rules allow some additions or changes. Keep the lease, receipts, and old orders. Keep proof to assess the home. Both sides should have a chance to respond. Ask the Controller's office where to apply. A local adviser can help too. Ask which papers and fees are needed. Check review and appeal deadlines too. Do not just cut rent based on a cheaper advert. An order need not start on the day it is made.
groups.source_review: Read official sections 7, 15, 16. Corrected statutory valuation and effective date rather than generic market-rent assumptions.
groups.notes: Replaced invented five-year method and no-retroactivity claim with actual formula and application-linked effective date.

groups.high: Structural alterations can affect a building's load paths, stability, fire safety, and services. Tenants should not remove walls, create openings, extend a building, or alter structural supports without confirming the lease, obtaining required owner consent, and securing applicable building or planning approvals. These are separate permissions: landlord agreement cannot waive a legal permit, and an authority's approval does not automatically amend a lease. In Bangladesh, Transfer of Property Act section 108(p), subject to its context and exceptions, restricts erecting permanent structures without the lessor's consent, with an agricultural-purpose exception. It is not a universal rule requiring two approvals for every minor repair. A qualified engineer should assess structural work and safe construction methods; do not infer that a wall is non-load-bearing from appearance. Obtain a written scope and preserve drawings, permissions, and completion records. Unauthorized work can lead to repair costs, contractual action, enforcement, or insurance disputes, depending on law and policy. Retrospective approval and insurance consequences are not identical everywhere. Stop and obtain expert advice if work reveals cracks, instability, or unknown structural elements.
groups.mid: Changing a wall, support, or opening can affect a building's strength. Fire safety and services can change too. Check the lease first. Get the owner's consent where needed. Get building or planning approval if the law requires it. These are separate permissions. The owner cannot waive a legal permit. A permit does not change the lease by itself. Bangladesh's Transfer of Property Act has a rule in section 108(p). It limits new permanent structures without the owner's consent. It has an exception for farming uses. Other conditions can matter. A small repair may not need both. Ask a trained engineer to check the structural work. Ask how to do it safely. You cannot tell by sight that a wall is safe to remove. Put the work plan in writing. Keep drawings, permissions, and completion records. Work without consent may lead to repair costs, lease action, enforcement, or insurance disputes. Law and policy decide the result. Later approval and insurance rules vary by place. If work reveals cracks, movement, or unknown supports, stop. Get expert help.
groups.low: Changing a wall, support, or opening can affect a building's strength. It can affect fire safety and services too. Check the lease first. Get the owner's consent where needed. Get building or planning approval if law requires it. These permissions differ. An owner cannot waive a legal permit. A permit does not change your lease by itself. Bangladesh's Transfer of Property Act has a rule in section 108(p). It limits new permanent structures without owner consent. There is an exception for farming uses. Other conditions may matter. A small repair may not need both. Ask a trained engineer to check the work. Ask how to do it safely. You cannot tell by sight that a wall is safe to remove. Write down the plan. Keep drawings, permissions, and completion records. Work without consent may bring repair costs or lease action. It may bring enforcement or insurance disputes too. Law and policy decide the result. Rules for later approval and insurance differ. Stop if work shows cracks, movement, or unknown supports. Get expert help.
groups.source_review: Checked Bangladesh section 108(p); local building approval and insurance effects explicitly left subject to jurisdiction and policy rather than asserted universally.
groups.notes: Corrected absolute dual-approval, invalid retrospective approval, universal full-liability, and automatic insurance-voidance claims.
